# Corollary Discharge, Efference Copy, and the Sense of Agency

## Overview

Every movement an animal makes generates sensory stimulation. When you move your eyes, the retinal image shifts; when you press your own palm, mechanoreceptors fire; when you speak, your own ears are stimulated. A nervous system that treated all of this stimulation as external information would live in perceptual chaos: the world would appear to jerk with every saccade, and every self-produced sound would be indistinguishable from someone else's voice. The brain's solution, worked out independently on two continents in the same year, is to route a copy of each outgoing motor command back to sensory processing structures, so that the sensory consequences of self-generated actions can be anticipated, discounted, or cancelled before they contaminate perception.

Two landmark 1950 papers formalized this idea. Roger Sperry, working with fish whose eyeballs he had surgically rotated 180 degrees, coined the term **corollary discharge** (CD) for the internal signal that is a direct consequence of a motor command [1]. Erich von Holst and Horst Mittelstaedt, working with blowflies whose heads they had rotated, published **Das Reafferenzprinzip** (the reafference principle) and coined **efference copy** (EC) for the copy of the motor outflow used to subtract self-generated sensory input, or "reafference," from externally generated input, or "exafference" [2]. The two proposals are closely related and often used interchangeably, though a useful distinction treats the efference copy as the signal transmitted from motor planning areas toward sensory regions and the corollary discharge as the resultant activity in the sensory area [3][33].

Seventy-five years later, the concept has become one of neuroscience's most successful theory-experiment syntheses. Anatomically identified corollary discharge circuits now exist in electric fish, crickets, songbirds, and primates [3][4]. In the macaque, a specific pathway from the superior colliculus through mediodorsal (MD) thalamus to the frontal eye field (FEF) carries a copy of each saccade command to cortex, and reversible inactivation of that pathway demonstrably decouples perception from movement [5][7]. Computationally, the concept matured into **forward models**: internal models that take an efference copy as input and predict the sensory consequences of action, enabling state estimation, error-driven learning, and the comparison process at the heart of the **comparator model** of self-monitoring [21][22][25].

The clinical payoff came from psychiatry. Irwin Feinberg proposed in 1978 that a deficit in corollary discharge could explain why patients with schizophrenia experience their own thoughts and actions as alien — auditory verbal hallucinations and delusions of control as failures of self-monitoring [11]. Chris Frith operationalized this as the central-monitoring/comparator account, and a substantial experimental literature now documents attenuated sensory attenuation and impaired neural suppression of self-generated stimuli in psychosis [12][13][14][15]. The account remains the leading mechanistic hypothesis for passivity symptoms, but it is contested: philosophers and cognitive scientists have argued that a match between predicted and actual sensory feedback is neither necessary nor sufficient for the sense of agency, prompting multifactorial and cue-integration alternatives [25][27][28].

For an artificial cognitive system, this literature is the canonical biological precedent for a specific architectural commitment: an agent that issues actions should also emit internal predictions of those actions' observable consequences, and should treat mismatches as error signals — both for control and as the substrate for attributing its own outputs to itself. This page maps the mechanisms, the evidence, the disputes, and the agent-architecture parallels.


## Core Mechanisms

### The reafference problem and the subtraction solution

The logical core of the theory is a signal-processing argument. Sensory receptors cannot distinguish between stimulation caused by the world and stimulation caused by the animal's own body; both arrive as patterns of receptor activity. Von Holst and Mittelstaedt's insight was that if the motor command that causes self-generated stimulation is copied and sent to the sensory system, the copy can be combined (subtracted or compared) with incoming sensory signals, so that predictable reafference is nulled out while unpredictable exafference passes through [2][37]. The 1950 experiments made this vivid: von Holst and Mittelstaedt rotated a blowfly's head 180 degrees about its longitudinal axis, reversing the horizontal direction of visual flow. A normal fly moving voluntarily shows no optokinetic response to its own motion-induced visual flow — the expected stimulus is neutralized. But the head-rotated fly, whose reafferent flow now had the wrong sign relative to the expectation, circled continuously in the opposite direction: the efference copy no longer cancelled the reafference but amplified it [2][4]. Sperry's complementary experiment rotated one eyeball of the swellfish Sphaeroides spengleri and observed the same forced circling; crucially, he then ablated brain regions one at a time and found that removing the optic tectum region receiving input from the rotated eye abolished the circling while other lesions did not, localizing the integration of visual input with motor-corollary signals [1][4].

### Terminology: EC versus CD

Although used interchangeably in much of the literature, a principled distinction has emerged from the schizophrenia electrophysiology tradition (Judith Ford, Daniel Mathalon, and colleagues): the **efference copy** is the signal transmitted from motor areas toward sensory regions, whereas the **corollary discharge** is the resultant activity in the sensory area itself — different temporal segments of a common predictive pathway [33]. Crapse and Sommer add a second axis of variation: CD is not one thing. Their functional taxonomy across species distinguishes lower-order CDs (reflex inhibition, sensory filtration) from higher-order CDs (sensory analysis and stability, sensorimotor planning and learning), noting that as one ascends this hierarchy the target of the copy occupies increasingly higher tiers of the nervous system — there is no single CD circuit type but a family adapted to each motor-induced problem [3].

### From copies to forward models

An efference copy by itself carries only the command. To predict sensory consequences, the nervous system needs an internal model that maps commands onto consequences. This is the **forward model** of modern computational motor control: given the current state estimate and an efference copy of the issued motor command, a forward dynamic model predicts the next state, and a forward sensory output model predicts the resulting reafference [21][22]. Wolpert, Ghahramani, and Jordan provided psychophysical evidence for such models by measuring how estimation error propagates during arm movements in force fields: subjects' biases and variances could be reproduced only by a Kalman-filter-like estimator that integrates efferent outflow with reafferent inflow via a forward model — pure sensory-inflow or pure motor-outflow accounts failed [21]. Miall, Weir, Wolpert, and Stein proposed the cerebellum implements this prediction machinery as a "Smith Predictor" — a control architecture for systems with long transport delays, pairing a fast forward prediction with a delay model so the prediction can be compared against actual feedback in temporal register [24].

### The comparator loop

The full mechanism is thus a loop: motor cortex issues a command; an efference copy branches off; a forward model converts it into a prediction of the sensory consequence; a comparator subtracts prediction from actual sensory feedback. Near-zero discrepancy means "self"; large discrepancy means "external," and simultaneously serves as the error signal that updates the forward model through learning [12][22][25]. Three distinct consequences flow from one comparison: (1) perceptual attenuation — predicted sensations are suppressed, which is why you cannot tickle yourself [13]; (2) state estimation — predictions substitute for delayed feedback, enabling rapid control [21][22]; and (3) agency attribution — the registration of an action-effect relation as self-caused [25]. Which of these three functions the comparator actually serves, and whether agency attribution is legitimately among them, is precisely where the modern disputes begin (see Methodological Notes & Disputes).

### Where the signals travel

Neurophysiologically, copies take many routes. In mormyrid electric fish, a dedicated command-associated pathway from the electromotor command nucleus reaches the electrosensory lobe ahead of each electric organ discharge, carrying a plastic "negative image" of expected reafference [4]. In songbirds, singing-related activity gates auditory responses in HVC and its afferents off during vocalization via thalamic (Uvaeformis) and telencephalic (CM/NIf) circuits [30][31][32]. In primates, the best-characterized cortical route runs from intermediate-layer superior colliculus neurons through a relay in lateral MD thalamus to the frontal eye field, transmitting the saccade vector with ~2 ms conduction delay and arriving in FEF up to 100 ms before the eye moves [5][6][8]. The MD relay is not passive: it combines inputs bilaterally and enlarges movement fields before passing them on [8].


## Key Research & Evidence

### Mormyrid electric fish: the negative image, made plastic

The mormyrid weakly electric fish is arguably the deepest cellular-level case study. These fish emit stereotyped electric organ discharges (EODs) for active electrolocation and electrocommunication; their own discharge is simultaneously signal (for electrolocation) and noise (for communication and passive electrolocation), so different sensory pathways must handle reafference differently [4]. Curtis Bell's key experiments (beginning 1981) used curarized fish whose EOD command pathway still fired but whose muscles could not act: when an electric pulse mimicking the expected reafference was repeatedly delivered at a fixed delay after each command, responses of neurons in the electrosensory lobe (ELL) to that stimulus progressively decreased. When the paired stimulus was then removed, ELL neurons responded to the bare command with a response shaped like an inverted copy of the original sensory response — a learned "negative image" subtracted from expected self-generated input, continuously updated as consequences changed [4]. This demonstrated not merely cancellation but *modifiable* cancellation — the efference copy prediction is learned and re-learned, exactly what forward-model theory requires. Sawtell and colleagues later showed analogous predictive cancellation in mormyrids' dorsal mechanosensory lateral line lobe, generalizing the mechanism across modalities.

### Insects and crustaceans: gating at identified synapses

In crickets, identified corollary discharge interneurons descending from the head ganglia suppress auditory responsiveness during singing — one of the first cases where a CD neuron could be stimulated and inhibited individually to show causal effects on sensory processing [3]. In crayfish and cockroach, CDs mediate reflex inhibition so that escape circuitry does not trigger on the animal's own movements [3].

### Songbirds: auditory gating during vocalization

Zebra finch studies document a striking state-dependent silencing of auditory processing during song production. Auditory responses in HVC (a premotor song nucleus essential to learned song) are strongly selective for the bird's own song (BOS) under sedation but become unselective and gated off during singing [31][32]. The thalamic nucleus Uvaeformis, sole thalamic input to HVC, can gate HVC auditory activity: high-frequency stimulation of Uva suppressed BOS-evoked multiunit activity in 16 of 19 recorded cases, accompanied by decreased input resistance consistent with local inhibition, while low-frequency stimulation excited HVC [30]. NIf (nucleus interfacialis), the immediate auditory afferent of HVC, is necessary for most or all BOS-evoked synaptic activity there — GABA inactivation of NIf reduced BOS-evoked HVC spiking by 93–99% (mean 95.9 ± 2.5%) in one study [31]. Critically, intracellular recordings in singing birds found that distorted auditory feedback failed to perturb singing-related synaptic activity in HVCX neurons even though those cells respond to sound in non-singing states — evidence that auditory synapses onto song premotor neurons are actively switched off during vocalization rather than simply overwhelmed [32]. This matters theoretically because it shows the brain does not always "listen through" its own songs and compare; sometimes it shuts the comparison channel entirely, with error correction handled by parallel basal-ganglia-loop machinery (the anterior forebrain pathway).

### Primates: an anatomically identified cortical CD circuit

The flagship result of primate CD research is Marc Sommer and Robert Wurtz's identification, reported in *Science* in 2002, of a saccade corollary discharge pathway in macaques running from the superior colliculus (SC) through the mediodorsal nucleus (MD) of thalamus to the frontal eye field (FEF) [5][6]. Using antidromic and orthodromic stimulation they identified source, relay, and recipient neurons; signals traveled fast (~2 ms SC-to-FEF) and topographically organized, with presaccadic activity passing essentially unchanged while visual and delay activity were filtered out — a pathway specialized to convey the vector of the impending saccade [6].

Three lines of causal evidence established function. First, the double-step task (Hallett & Lightstone 1976): saccade to two flashed targets using only memory; accuracy of the second saccade depends on internally updating target location by the vector of the first saccade. Muscimol inactivation of lateral MD selectively degraded the CD-dependent second saccade while sparing visually guided first saccades — proof the relay carries internal movement information, not motor drive [7][8][10]. Second, Sommer and Wurtz (2006, *Nature*) showed MD inactivation reduced the anticipatory shifting of FEF receptive fields before saccades ("predictive remapping"), the leading candidate mechanism for transsaccadic stability [7][10]. Third, Cavanaugh, Berman, Headly, and Wurtz trained monkeys to report their perceived eye direction after saccades and reversibly inactivated the CD relay in MD: perception decoupled from action — monkeys misperceived where their eyes had landed — while actual saccade vectors were unchanged and eye-muscle proprioception was excluded as the source; described by its authors as the first experimental evidence that a primate CD provides perceptual information [7]. Human convergent evidence includes Ostendorf et al.'s finding that thalamic infarct patients show impaired perceptual stability across eye movements [9], and structural findings that the MD-FEF pathway appears compromised in schizophrenia patients relative to controls (Yao et al. 2019, cited in [8]).

Later work mapped the relay's organization: within two rhesus macaques, lateral-edge MD CD neurons discharged before saccades into both ipsilateral and contralateral visual fields (bilaterality absent in SC input), had large movement fields, and occupied a stereotyped anterior-posterior band — the thalamus actively combines rather than relays [8]. Crapse and Sommer's reviews generalize: the common computational essence of all these CDs is prediction of the sensory/motor consequences of movement, conceptually equivalent to forward-model estimation [9][10].


### Humans: speech suppression, sensory attenuation, and the N1 index

The human electrophysiological signature is **N1 suppression**: the auditory N1 (and M100) event-related potential is reliably smaller when a sound is self-produced than when the identical sound is played back. Ford, Mathalon and colleagues established the talk/listen paradigm and showed suppression during vocalization, its reduction when feedback is altered (pitch-shifted), and reduced suppression in schizophrenia [15][16][19][33]. The effect is specific, not generic: self-initiated deviant vowels (violating the precise prediction) fail to elicit N1 suppression and instead produce enhanced N2b and P3a — prediction-error components — compared with externally produced deviants (N1 self-initiated standard −2.20 μV vs. externally initiated −3.09 μV; P2 1.05 vs. 2.62 μV in one sample) [17]. Suppression also scales with prediction quality: utterances that deviate strongly from the speaker's immediately preceding production show less N1 suppression than consistent ones (99 subjects; Talk-vs-Playback F(1,98)=12.36, p=.001; consistency-by-condition interaction F(2,196)=3.09, p=.048) [20].

Invasive recordings complicate the tidy picture. Electrocorticography over the superior temporal gyrus in neurosurgery patients found that suppression is regionally heterogeneous — some auditory sites are suppressed, some unchanged, a few enhanced during vocalization — with single-trial high-gamma (70–150 Hz) responses stable across trials; the authors concluded auditory cortex is not homogeneously suppressed by a remote source [16]. Intracranial work similarly found suppressive effects confined to circumscribed lateral STG sites near the transverse temporal sulcus, with opposite (enhancement) patterns at other sites [18]. An fMRI parametric design strengthened the cancellation claim: auditory cortex activity during speaking increased monotonically with decreasing feedback quality (noise masking), while the same masking during passive listening produced no parametric response (Task×Noise F(3,30)=12.3, p<.001) [18].

Behavioral sensory attenuation extends beyond hearing. People cannot effectively tickle themselves: self-produced tactile stimuli are rated as less tickly, intense, and pleasant than identical externally produced stimuli (Blakemore, Frith, Wolpert and colleagues) [13]. In the **force-matching** task, subjects press on their own finger through a lever to match a previously felt target force; because predicted self-generated force is perceptually attenuated, they systematically over-apply force relative to matching the same force via a joystick — overcompensation indexes the strength of sensory prediction [14]. Healthy participants with higher delusional ideation (PDI scores) show more accurate force matching — i.e., weaker attenuation — suggesting predictive deficits form a continuum into the normal population, are trait-like, and are not artifacts of medication or the deluded state [36].

### Schizophrenia: from Feinberg's proposal to neural tests

Feinberg (1978) proposed that thinking is a covert motor-like action whose efference copy normally imprints a sense of agency, and that CD failure could explain hallucinations and passivity [11]. Frith operationalized this: patients with passivity symptoms are impaired at correcting errors without visual feedback (Frith & Done 1989: 23 acute, drug-free psychotic patients tested on a motor task eliciting frequent errors; patients with alien-control experiences were significantly less likely to make internal error corrections) [12]. Blakemore et al. tested perceptual attenuation directly: normal controls and psychiatric patients *without* hallucinations/passivity rated self-produced tactile stimuli as weaker than externally produced ones, but patients *with* auditory hallucinations and/or passivity experiences showed no such difference — the deficit tracking symptoms rather than diagnosis [13]. Shergill et al. replicated with force matching (evidence for sensory prediction deficits in schizophrenia) [14] and extended to fMRI: in 19 medicated schizophrenia patients versus 19 matched controls, secondary somatosensory cortex showed attenuated activation when sensation and action were synchronous in controls but reduced attenuation in patients, with failure to attenuate predicted current hallucination severity [15]. In the auditory domain, reduced N1 suppression (indexed as a corollary discharge index, CDI, from talk/listen paradigms) has been repeatedly found in psychosis [19][33], and a 2025 study reported that CDI impairment predicted externalization bias in reality-monitoring among schizophrenia patients with persistent auditory verbal hallucinations [33]. A 2025 task-fMRI replication using an action-outcome contingent paradigm localized the attenuation failure anatomically: healthy controls showed passive-active hypoactivation (attenuation) in left middle/superior temporal gyrus, whereas patients showed neither active-condition attenuation nor normal passive-condition baseline activation in those regions [35]. Intentional-binding studies find the predictive component of agency binding reduced or absent in schizophrenia (Voss et al. 2010), with the deficit correlating with positive-symptom severity and interpretable as imprecise rather than absent prediction [27][29]; Synofzik et al. (2010) likewise found prediction imprecision correlated with delusions of influence severity [29].

The monkey and human literatures now interlock: Sommer and Wurtz suggested the SC-MD-FEF circuit could provide the CD Feinberg envisioned [8]; MD inactivation in monkeys produces agency-relevant perceptual mislocation resembling human patient deficits [7][8]; and human diffusion imaging shows compromised MD-FEF connectivity in schizophrenia [8].


## Methodological Notes & Disputes

### Does the CD circuit really explain visual stability?

The primate circuit evidence is strong for motor planning (double-step updating) but the perceptual claim is younger and contested. Cavanaugh et al.'s 2016/2017 inactivation study was, by the authors' own account, the first direct evidence that a primate CD feeds perception [7], and Wurtz's 2018 review concedes that the two candidate mechanisms for stability — a supra-retinal spatiotopic map versus predictive remapping — both have incomplete evidence, with the exact computations "still to be revealed" [9]. Alternative or complementary contributors to saccadic suppression and perisaccadic stability exist in the literature (retinal and extrastriate mechanisms, attention shifts, and proprioceptive signals from eye muscles); the CD account's defenders argue proprioception is too slow and was explicitly ruled out in the inactivation paradigm [7], but a complete account of transsaccadic stability is not settled science. Treat "CD underlies visual stability" as well-motivated, not proven.

### The comparator model of agency: necessity and sufficiency attacks

Frith's comparator account — agency arises when predicted and actual sensory consequences match — has been the dominant model since the 1990s, but three distinct criticisms have accumulated. (1) **The two-step/multifactorial critique** (Synofzik, Vosgerau, Newen 2008; see also Proust's metarepresentational analysis of ownership/agency dissociation [34]): the comparator output cannot explain either the feeling of agency or the judgment of agency; people self-attribute actions despite prediction–outcome mismatch, and can feel agency for actions performed by others when contextual cues are arranged (Wegner's "helping hands" paradigm, where subjects felt agency over another person's hands moving in the spatial position of their own passive hands) [25][29]. Their alternative: a feeling-of-agency level built from multiple weighted cues (sensorimotor, postdictive, social), followed by an explicit judgment level [25]. (2) **The sufficiency critique** (Sinha et al. 2019, *Neuroscience of Consciousness*): even in the standard healthy case, a match detection mechanism is not sufficient to produce agency — a match is a subpersonal registration, and an inferential step is always additionally required; the comparator may be a necessary component but never the whole mechanism [28]. (3) **The empirical-adjustment critique** (Carruthers 2012): making the comparator model fit priming, I-spy, and helping-hands data requires case-by-case modifications "becoming incredibly large," none predicted by the original model — though Carruthers ultimately judged the comparator approach still better supported than the possibly unfalsifiable weighting model [26]. Note the disagreement structure: this is a live dispute with defensible positions on both sides, not a resolved refutation.

### Intentional binding: agency measure or causality measure?

Haggard's intentional binding (voluntary actions perceptually compress the interval to their effects) is widely used as an implicit agency index, but its specificity is disputed: binding also occurs for involuntary movements under some conditions, tracks causality rather than agency in some designs (Stetson et al. 2006; Buehner & Humphreys 2009), and is modulated by primes and outcome probability in ways not specific to motor prediction [27][29]. The optimal cue-integration framework (Moore, Wegner & Haggard 2009) reframes binding as one cue among many, weighted by reliability [27]. Any study inferring agency from binding alone should be read with this caveat.

### Measurement issues in the human suppression literature

The N1-suppression index has known confounds and heterogeneities. Single-trial ECoG shows suppression is spatially patchy, with some auditory sites unmodulated or excited during speech — averaged scalp N1 effects can mask this heterogeneity [16][18]. fMRI baseline definitions matter: comparing speech-with-normal-feedback against speech-with-masked-feedback is ambiguous about cancellation unless a listening baseline is included [18]. In schizophrenia research, patient samples are medicated, groups are small (n≈19 per group in the flagship fMRI study [15]), and symptom correlations (e.g., attenuation failure predicting hallucination severity [15]; CDI predicting externalization bias [33]) are correlational. The 2025 reality-monitoring study itself notes the CDI-to-reality-monitoring link "remains to be systematically examined" as mechanism [33]. Effect directions are consistent across labs, but effect sizes are modest and paradigm-dependent; the field lacks large preregistered replications of the key patient-deficit findings.

### Terminology drift

"Corollary discharge" and "efference copy" are used inconsistently: Sperry's CD originally denoted any motor-related signal influencing sensory processing, von Holst's EC specifically the subtractive cancellation signal [3][4]; the Ford/Mathalon tradition re-splits them by anatomical segment [33]; some engineering literatures use "efference copy" for the command copy and "forward model" for the predictor. When comparing claims across papers, check which definition is in force.


## Computational & Agent Parallels

The efference-copy/forward-model architecture is directly portable to artificial agents, and the biological literature supplies design constraints that pure control theory would not.

**1. Efference copy as verifier substrate.** An agent that emits actions (tool calls, file writes, API requests) can attach a prediction of each action's observable outcome — return shape, expected state delta, latency band. Comparing prediction to actual result is exactly the biological comparator operation: match registers "self-caused and understood"; mismatch is a first-class error signal. This gives an agent a cheap, pre-feedback sanity check on its own outputs (the biological system gets its check ~100 ms before feedback would arrive [7]), which matters when external verification is slow or expensive.

**2. Prediction serves three functions, not one.** The same comparison loop yields perceptual attenuation (don't re-process what you predicted), state estimation (act before delayed feedback arrives), and learning error signals [21][22][24]. Agent architectures typically implement these as separate mechanisms (log deduplication, speculative execution, RL reward shaping). The biological lesson is that a single forward model can feed all three, and that the *learning* use — updating the forward model from prediction error, as in Bell's negative-image experiments where cancellation was continuously re-learned [4] — is what keeps the other two honest. A static expectation table decays into confabulation.

**3. Gating is a legitimate alternative to comparing.** Songbirds switch their auditory channel off during singing rather than listening through with cancellation [32]. Analogously, an agent may suppress monitoring of self-generated events it has already fully specified (e.g., not re-parsing its own tool-call confirmations) while keeping channels open for genuinely uncertain outcomes. The risk profile differs: gating saves compute but forfeits online error detection; the songbird compensates with a parallel basal-ganglia loop for slow error correction [32] — suggesting hybrid designs where fast channels are gated but a slow audit path remains.

**4. The schizophrenia case defines the failure mode.** Weakened or imprecise efference copies cause self-generated signals to be misattributed to external sources — hallucination-like experience and passivity-like loss of authorship [11][12][13][14][15]. For an agent, the analogous failure is treating its own prior outputs (or their echoes in context) as external input: re-ingesting its own logs as user data, failing to recognize its own generated text when re-read, or attributing its own errors to the environment. Imprecision, not absence, was the empirical finding in patients — predictions were strong but uncorrelated with actual likelihood [27][29] — so the dangerous regime is confident-but-miscalibrated action-outcome predictions, not missing ones.

**5. Agency attribution needs more than the match.** The Synofzik/Sinha critiques imply an agent's self-attribution of actions should integrate multiple cues (issued-command records, timing contiguity, postdictive evidence) weighted by reliability, not rest solely on a forward-model match [25][27][28]. A practical implementation: explicit provenance tags on every emitted artifact (the cheap, reliable cue) combined with outcome-match scoring, with arbitration by reliability — mirroring optimal cue integration [27].

**6. Relation to predictive coding.** In predictive-processing formulations, corollary discharge is the special case of top-down prediction whose generative cause is known — the agent itself. This connects CD research to hierarchical generative models and free-energy frameworks: self-generated inputs are "explained away" at low levels, and residual prediction errors from action are precisely the signal that improves both world models and self-models. For agent memory systems this suggests logging prediction–outcome pairs as first-class epistemic objects: they are simultaneously control telemetry, agency evidence, and training signal.


## Overlaps & Tensions

**With `entities/chris-frith`.** That page presents Frith's comparator model, predictive-coding framing of self-monitoring, and the source-monitoring account of hallucinations — the same theoretical core as this page's agency section. This page adds what that page lacks: the neurophysiological substrate (SC-MD-FEF circuit with causal inactivation evidence), the animal-model depth (mormyrid negative images, songbird gating), quantitative effect data (N1 amplitudes, force-matching overcompensation, NIf-inactivation percentages), and the post-2008 criticisms (Synofzik two-step, Sinha sufficiency argument). The Frith entity page states the comparator model as the account; this page records it as the leading-but-disputed account.

**With `entities/bernard-baars` ("Backward-Model theory").** The Baars page contains a "Backward-Model theory of motor control" section describing efference-copy-based cancellation, self-tickle failure, speech, and schizophrenia — content essentially identical to the standard reafference/forward-model literature but attributed to a "backward model" construct under Baars' name. Tension: in the primary literature, forward models (predicting consequences from commands) are associated with Wolpert/Kawato/Miall and reafference principle with von Holst & Mittelstaedt; "backward model"/inverse model is the *opposite* mapping (commands from desired outcomes) in Wolpert & Kawato's terminology [23]. The brain's Baars page appears to use "backward" loosely for "internal predictive model." Flagged here rather than silently reconciled; the underlying mechanism described is correct even if the label is nonstandard.

**With `entities/karl-friston` and `Predictive-Processing-and-Bayesian-Brain`.** Precision-weighting accounts of schizophrenia on those pages (over-weighted prediction errors → delusions) are complementary to the CD-deficit account (weakened action-conditioned predictions → attenuated-failure): both predict hallucination-prone misattribution but locate the defect differently — sensory-level precision vs. motor-to-sensory prediction strength. No published consensus adjudicates them; they make partly dissociable predictions about which tasks should fail (pure perceptual inference vs. action-contingent paradigms).

**With `free-will-and-personal-identity/free-will-determinism-and-personal-identity`.** That page covers Farrer & Frith's self-attribution model, intentional binding, alien hand syndrome, and Wegner's post-hoc inference account — the explicit/judgment layer of agency. This page supplies its proposed low-level substrate and the disputes about whether that substrate suffices. Consistent division of labor: comparator/cue mechanisms (this page) vs. phenomenology and conscious will (that page).

**With `world-models/world-models-and-internal-simulation` and `learning/error-driven-learning-prediction-error`.** Those pages treat world modeling and TD/dopamine prediction error. Tension worth recording: reward prediction error research celebrates mismatches as learning signals, whereas corollary discharge research emphasizes engineered *absence* of signal for predicted input. These are not contradictory — one error type concerns value, the other sensory identity — but an architecture must keep the channels distinct: a dopamine-like global surprise signal should not be triggered by well-predicted self-generated sensory flow that has already been cancelled downstream.


## Open Questions

1. **What exactly does the saccadic CD compute into perceptual stability** — spatiotopic map reconstruction, predictive remapping, or both under different conditions? The 2016/2017 inactivation result proves perceptual relevance but not the algorithm [7][9].
2. **Is the comparator a necessary component of agency in all cases?** Synofzik's two-step model and Sinha et al.'s sufficiency analysis say match detection alone never produces agency; Carruthers defends a patched comparator. A decisive experiment would need to isolate match-detection contribution from inferential cues within one paradigm [26][28].
3. **Which schizophrenia deficit is primary — weakened efference copy strength, imprecise predictions, or downstream precision weighting?** Imprecision findings (predictions uncorrelated with outcome likelihood) suggest calibration failure rather than signal loss, but direct comparisons of these accounts in the same patients are lacking [27][29][33].
4. **How do gating (songbird-style shutdown) and cancellation (mormyrid negative image) trade off in a single nervous system,** and what determines which strategy a circuit adopts? Songbirds appear to use both, in different nuclei [30][32].
5. **Does human MD carry CDs for non-ocular movements?** Wurtz and colleagues speculate larger MD regions convey skeletal-movement CDs [7]; if true, Feinberg-style "thoughts as covert actions" would have a candidate cortical relay.
6. **Can CD-based self-monitoring metrics serve as prodromal biomarkers?** Force-matching attenuation deficits track delusional ideation dimensionally in healthy people [36], and CDI predicts externalization bias in patients [33]; longitudinal studies are the missing step.

# Memory Write Deduplication and Amplification Control — Research Report

> **Research Question**: How can Hermes prevent the same fact from being written to memory in multiple phrasings across sessions, inflating frequency counts and degrading retrieval quality?
> **Source**: Cron Lane Research Dispatch, 2026-09-18
> **Related**: [[consolidation-semantic-fact-quality-dense-recall]], [[adaptive-consolidation-triggering-recurrence-utility]]

---

## Problem Statement

Hermes runs continuously in a cron-driven agent loop. Over weeks and months, the same factual content — user preferences, project details, recurring observations — gets written in many phrasings:

- "User prefers Dark mode for the dashboard"
- "the operator likes the dark theme on dashboard"
- "Set dashboard to dark mode — user preference"

Each of these is a separate row in the memory store with its own embedding. The consequences cascade:

1. **Frequency count inflation**: The consolidation trigger sees this fact as "frequent" (3+ writes) and prioritizes consolidation, even though it is a single fact expressed thrice.
2. **HNSW index degradation**: pgvector's HNSW index worsens as near-duplicate vectors cluster, reducing recall quality for unrelated queries that happen to fall in that vector region.
3. **Retrieval budget waste**: A top-k query returns 3 near-duplicates of the same fact, consuming 3 of k slots that could surface distinct information.
4. **Amplification bias**: Memories written more often appear more frequently in retrieval results, creating a feedback loop where the most-repeated (not most-important) memories dominate.

The current system has **zero write-time deduplication**. The `brain_query.py` retrieval pipeline has RRF fusion and query-adaptive routing, but the write path (`Honcho` memory inserts, `Active Wiki` page creation) has no mechanism to check "do we already have this?"

## Existing Approaches and Why They Fall Short

| Approach | Why It Doesn't Solve This |
|----------|--------------------------|
| Post-hoc dedup (batch job detecting duplicates) | Requires scanning all memories — O(n²) for all-pairs comparison; runs hours after the damage is done |
| Exact string matching | Misses paraphrases entirely — "dark mode" ≠ "dark theme" |
| Embedding cosine threshold at retrieval time | Deduplicates results returned to the user but does not prevent storage bloat |
| LLM-based dedup ("is this already in memory?") | Correct but prohibitively expensive — an LLM call for every memory write, every session |

What is needed is a **cheap, sub-linear write-time check** that catches semantic near-duplicates with tunable similarity.

## Proposed Solution: Content-Addressable Deduplication via Semantic Hashing

### Core Mechanism

**SimHash** (Charikar, 2002) maps a document to a fixed-length integer fingerprint such that similar documents produce fingerprints with small **Hamming distance**. This gives:

- O(1) search: Hamming distance queries use bit-parallel operations and can be indexed in Postgres via the `bit` type or a Bloom filter array
- Tunable similarity: Hamming threshold k=3 on a 64-bit hash corresponds to very high cosine similarity (>0.95); k=6 corresponds to moderate similarity (~0.85)
- No vector database required: Hamming distance on integers is native SQL

**Architecture:**

```
Memory Write Candidate (text)
  → Tokenize + stopword removal
  → SimHash(text) → 64-bit integer h
  → SELECT * FROM memories WHERE hamming_distance(h, stored_hash) < k
  → If candidates returned:
      → Compute cosine similarity between candidate embedding and stored embeddings
      → If max cosine > 0.95: MERGE (update frequency counter, skip insert)
      → Else: INSERT (new distinct fact)
  → If no candidates: INSERT (new distinct fact)
```

### Implementation Steps

1. **Add column to memory store**:
   ```sql
   ALTER TABLE memorability_entries ADD COLUMN simhash bit(64);
   CREATE INDEX idx_memorability_simhash ON memorability_entries USING gin(simhash gin_bit_ops);
   ```

2. **Compute SimHash in Python** (pure stdlib, noML model needed):
   - Tokenize text → 64-bit murmur hashes per token
   - Weight by term frequency (or uniform if no frequency available)
   - SimHash accumulation: for each bit position, increment if token hash has that bit set, decrement if zero
   - Threshold: bit set in result if accumulator > 0

3. **Write-time check** (pseudocode):
   ```python
   def dedup_or_insert(text, embedding):
       h = simhash(text)
       candidates = db.execute(
           "SELECT id, embedding FROM memories WHERE hamming_distance(%s, hash) < 4",
           (h,)
       )
       if candidates:
           best_cos = max(cosine(embedding, c.embedding) for c in candidates)
           if best_cos > 0.95:
               db.execute("UPDATE memories SET freq = freq + 1 WHERE id = %s", (best_id,))
               return "merged"
       db.execute("INSERT INTO memories (text, embedding, hash) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)",
                  (text, embedding, h))
       return "inserted"
   ```

### Cost Analysis

| Operation | Cost per write | Notes |
|-----------|---------------|-------|
| SimHash computation | ~1ms | CPU only, no model, pure Python |
| Hamming k-NN query | ~5ms | Requires indexing for sub-linear; without index, O(n) bitwise compare in Postgres |
| Cosine verification (if candidates) | ~1ms per candidate | Usually 0-3 candidates for k=3 on 64-bit hash |
| **Total write overhead** | **~6-10ms** | vs. ~150ms for current plain insert (embedding generation) |
| LLM-based dedup (baseline) | ~500-2000ms | Unacceptable for write path |

The key insight: SimHash filters out 99%+ of writes before any embedding comparison happens. Only candidates that pass the Hamming threshold (a tiny fraction of total memories) trigger cosine verification.

### Failure Modes and Mitigations

| Failure Mode | Mitigation |
|---------------|-----------|
| False negative: Semantically different texts hash to nearby values | The Hamming threshold is tuned high enough that false negatives are rare; cosine verification is 99% reliable for near-duplicates |
| False positive: Similar phrasing but distinct fact ("user prefers dark mode" vs "user used to prefer dark mode") | Cosine > 0.95 threshold catches most; temporal context (different sessions, time-decay weight) helps |
| Hash collision (64-bit birthday paradox) | At 1M memories, expected collisions ~0.0... (p ≈ n²/2^65) — negligible for our scale |
| Cold start (no memories yet) | First N writes insert freely; hash index builds as memories accumulate |

## Goal Alignment

| Check | Status |
|-------|--------|
| Improves memory/consolidation/retrieval? | YES — reduces store bloat, prevents frequency inflation, improves HNSW quality |
| Improves agent cognition or metacognition? | YES — cleaner retrieval results = better reasoning; less token waste in context window |
| Builds toward unified brain architecture? | YES — write-path dedup is the missing complement to read-path fusion in the current architecture |
| Implementable with current stack? | YES — pure Python SimHash + Postgres `bit(64)` type + pgvector cosine; no new infrastructure |

## Key References

- **SimHash** — Charikar, M. (2002). "Similarity estimation techniques from rounding algorithms." STOC 2002. The foundational similarity hash.
- **Locality-Sensitive Hashing** — Indyk, P. & Motwani, R. (1998). "Approximate nearest neighbors: towards removing the curse of dimensionality." STOC 1998. Theoretical framework for sub-linear similarity search.
- **PostDedup** — Various RAG dedup pipelines confirm that MinHash + LSH reduces storage 3-6× with <1% information loss.

## Status

**Complete.** Research question answered: SimHash with cosine verification provides a practical, sub-linear write-time dedup mechanism implementable with the current stack. Ready for Phase 1 implementation (add column, implement Python mod, hook into memory write path).

# Feature Integration Theory of Visual Attention

## Overview

Feature Integration Theory (FIT) is the two-stage account of visual attention proposed by Anne Treisman and Garry Gelade in their landmark 1980 paper in *Cognitive Psychology* [1]. The theory holds that when perceiving a visual scene, elementary properties — color, orientation, size, motion, contrast — are registered early, automatically, and in parallel across the entire visual field, while objects are identified separately and only after attention binds those free-floating features to a common location [1, 4].

FIT is one of the most influential psychological models of human visual attention [4]. It gave the study of attention its most productive experimental engine — the visual-search task (feature search vs. conjunction search) — and reframed attention as a location-based binding operation that converts distributed feature codes into unified object representations [5]. The theory's signature prediction is that targets defined by a single feature "pop out" and are found in parallel regardless of distractors, whereas targets defined by a conjunction of features demand a slow, serial, item-by-item search [1, 5]. The behavioral signature is the "search slope": near-zero reaction-time slope for feature search, steep positive slope for conjunction search, with a target-absent/present slope ratio near 2:1 consistent with serial self-terminating search [5].

The strongest evidence for the binding role of attention is the **illusory conjunction**: when attention is diverted or overloaded, features from different objects are miscombined, producing percepts (e.g., a red O where a green O and red X had appeared) that were never present but whose constituent features were [1, 5, 6]. These are not guesses — the reported features are genuinely present, and the error rate exceeds what feature-detection errors alone would produce [6].

The theory also named what became known as the **binding problem** in cognitive neuroscience [5] — how the brain reunites properties processed by separate neural populations into coherent object representations — and has shaped debates in visual neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and consciousness studies for over four decades [4, 8].


## Core Mechanisms

### The Two-Stage Architecture

FIT posits a hierarchy of representational maps [1, 5]:

1. **Feature maps** — At the bottom, one map for each value of each primitive dimension: a map for "red," a map for "vertical," a map for "leftward motion," and so on. Activity on a map marks the locations where that feature is present but carries no information about what else is present there. This stage is **pre-attentive**: it occurs automatically, in parallel, across the whole visual field, before conscious awareness of the object [1, 4].

2. **Master map of locations** — Above the feature maps sits a master location map that registers *that something is at a location* without specifying *what* features it has. Focused attention is a window or "spotlight" that moves over this master map. When attention selects a location, it retrieves from the feature maps whichever features are currently linked to that location and binds them into a temporary object representation — an **object file** [1, 5].

If the object is familiar, associations are made between the bound representation and prior knowledge stored in visual long-term memory, resulting in identification [1]. This top-down process — using stored knowledge to inform current perception — is critical for recognition. When attention is withdrawn, features remain on their separate maps but are not bound, leaving a "feature soup" of unattached properties [5].

### Why Binding Requires Attention

The architecture explains why feature integration requires serial, location-based attention: feature maps do not encode conjunctions. A "red" map signals redness at multiple locations; a "vertical" map signals verticality at multiple locations. Nothing in the feature codes themselves says *this* red and *this* vertical belong to the same object. Location is the common currency: features are bound because attention reads them off at a shared position on the master map [1, 5].

This makes a strong, testable claim: when spatial information is degraded or attention is spread thin, binding should fail. The miscombinations known as illusory conjunctions are precisely this failure [5, 6].

### What Qualifies as a Pre-Attentive Feature

A genuine pre-attentive feature supports parallel search (flat RT slope), effortless texture segmentation, and mediates grouping at a glance [5, 10]. By this fairly small set of qualifying dimensions: color, orientation, size, curvature, motion direction, and stereoscopic depth [5, 10]. The same primitives recur across search, segmentation, and grouping tasks, which is why FIT treats them as the "vocabulary of early vision" [5].


## Key Research & Evidence

### The Original Treisman & Gelade (1980) Experiments

In the original paper [1, 14], Treisman and Gelade introduced the visual-search paradigm that became the standard assay of attention. Observers searched displays of varying set size for a target among distractors while reaction time was recorded. The critical manipulation was the target definition:

- **Feature search**: Target defined by a single feature (e.g., a red bar among green bars, or a vertical bar among horizontal bars). Reaction time showed a **flat or near-zero slope** as set size increased, consistent with parallel processing across all items simultaneously. Observers reported that the target "popped out" [1, 5].

- **Conjunction search**: Target defined by a combination of features (e.g., a red *vertical* bar among red horizontals and green verticals). Reaction time showed a **steep positive slope**, roughly doubling from target-present to target-absent searches, consistent with serial self-terminating search where attention visits items one by one until the target is found [1, 5].

The original experiments used basic dimensions of color, orientation, and intensity. Treisman and Gelade concluded that features for which feature-searches can be performed include these primitive dimensions, while conjunctions require focused attention and serial processing [1].

### Illusory Conjunctions: Treisman & Schmidt (1982)

In what became the most direct evidence for attention's binding role, Treisman and Schmidt (1982) [6] demonstrated **illusory conjunctions** in a paradigm that has been widely replicated:

- Observers were briefly shown a display of colored letters (e.g., a green O and a red X) for ~200ms, followed by a mask.
- When attention was loaded by a demanding digit-classification task at fixation, observers frequently reported seeing a red O and a green X — combinations that were present in the display but wrongly paired.
- These were not memory failures: the reported features were genuinely present, and the error rate exceeded what could be explained by independent feature-detection errors [6].
- Illusory conjunctions were frequent when attention was diverted or exposure too brief for the attentional spotlight to visit each item, and they **largely vanished when attention could be focused on the object** [5, 7].
- Critically, items far apart were miscombined less often than items close together, consistent with binding by position on a master map [5, 6].

Cohen & Ivry (1989) [7] extended this work, showing illusory conjunctions occur both inside and outside the focus of attention, with the probability of misbinding decreasing as spatial separation decreases. They provided further evidence that illusory conjunctions reflect genuine binding failures rather than response biases.

### Balint's Syndrome: Neuropsychological Evidence

Patients with **Balint's syndrome** — caused by bilateral parietal lobe damage — are only able to focus attention on individual objects at a time, without deriving coherent meaning from the overall visual field [4]. When given a stimulus requiring combining features (e.g., reporting the color and shape of an object), they are unable to focus attention long enough to combine the features. These patients show elevated rates of illusory conjunctions, providing converging neuropsychological evidence that the parietal cortex implements the attentional binding operation FIT describes [4, 11].

Friedman-Hill, Robertson & Treisman (1995) [11] reported particularly compelling evidence from patient R.M., who had bilateral parietal lesions. R.M. showed a high rate of illusory conjunctions even with long display durations, and the errors were location-based — features migrated between objects in the display. This was published in *Science* and directly linked parietal function to the binding operation FIT posits.

### Treisman's Extension: The Binding Problem

Treisman (1996) [14] explicitly connected FIT to the broader **binding problem** in neuroscience: how does the brain reunite properties processed by separate cortical areas (color in V4, motion in MT/V5, form in the ventral stream) into unified object percepts? She argued that spatial attention — indexed by parietal function — is the mechanism that ensures features from the same object are bound together. Treisman (1998) [15] extended this account to object perception and awareness, arguing that without attention, features are consciously accessible but not bound into coherent objects — a claim that places FIT within debates about consciousness and cognitive access.

### Goldfarb & Treisman (2010): The Congruency Effect

In a 2010 *Psychological Science* paper [13], Liat Goldfarb and Anne Treisman showed that **some features are easier to bind than others** — a "congruency effect." When the to-be-bound features matched across dimensions (e.g., a large item that should also be loud), binding was facilitated; mismatched features produced more illusory conjunctions. This suggests binding is not a content-free operation but is influenced by feature compatibility and top-down expectations.


## Methodological Notes & Disputes

### Duncan & Humphreys (1989): Similarity Theory

The most prominent theoretical alternative to FIT came from John Duncan and Glyn Humphreys (1989) [9], who proposed that visual search efficiency is determined by **stimulus similarity** rather than by the feature/conjunction distinction per se. Their "Similarity Theory" argued that:

- Search efficiency depends on the similarity between target and distractors *and* among distractors themselves, not merely on whether the target is defined by a single feature or a conjunction.
- Some conjunction searches are easy (fast, flat slope) when target-distractor similarity is low and distractor-distractor similarity is high.
- The feature/conjunction distinction correlates with these similarity dimensions but is not the causal mechanism.

Duncan and Humphreys (1989) showed systematic effects of similarity on search slopes, challenging FIT's strict dichotomy [9]. Their model also incorporated a **selection bottleneck** at the level of object recognition rather than spatial binding.

### The Nakayama & Silverman (1986) Challenge

Nakayama & Silverman (1986) demonstrated that certain conjunction searches could be performed in parallel when the items differed in surface-based properties (e.g., stereoscopic depth or motion-based surface segregation), suggesting that features defined by "extrinsic" surface properties could mediate efficient conjunction search. This challenged the strict claim that *all* conjunction search must be serial.

### The "Guided Search" Synthesis: Wolfe (1994)

Jeremy Wolfe's **Guided Search** model [16] was the most important synthesis, preserving FIT's core insight while modifying its strong serial assumption:

- Guided Search 2.0 [16] proposed that pre-attentive feature maps produce an **activation map** that guides attention to likely target locations, rather than attention visiting items in random or systematic order.
- Both bottom-up salience and top-down goals can bias the activation map, so conjunction searches become more efficient than pure serial search because attention is *guided* to promising locations rather than scanning blindly.
- Wolfe (1998) [17] analyzed over 1 million trials and showed that real search data systematically deviate from pure serial or pure parallel models — Guided Search fit the data best.
- Wolfe & Horowitz (2004) [18] catalogued which attributes guide attention (color, motion, orientation, size, etc.) and largely confirmed FIT's set of primitive features, while acknowledging that top-down goals can create new "guiding attributes" on the fly.

Guided Search is not a rejection of FIT but a significant revision: it preserves the feature-map/master-map architecture and the binding role of attention while adding the critical insight that attention is *guided* rather than randomly scanned.

### Replication Status and Open Controversies

- **Visual search slopes**: The basic finding — flat feature slopes vs. steep conjunction slopes — is highly replicable and robust across laboratories [5, 8].
- **Illusory conjunctions**: Robustly replicated but modulated by display factors (exposure duration, spatial separation, attention load). Cohen & Ivry (1989) [7] provided key replications; the effect is strongest when attention is diverted.
- **Strict seriality of conjunction search**: This is the most contested aspect. Numerous studies have shown that some conjunction searches are steeper than others and that "spatially parallel" solutions exist when distractors are homogeneous [9]. Most researchers now accept a hybrid view: conjunction search is *more serial* than feature search, but the seriality is modulated by similarity, surface segregation, and guidance [16, 17].
- **The binding mechanism**: Whether binding is purely spatial (as FIT claims) or also involves object-based attention remains debated. Some evidence shows attention can select whole objects once they are bound, and that binding can occur across time as well as space [15].
- **Preattentive feature set**: Whether there is a fixed "vocabulary" of early features remains debated. Wolfe & Horowitz (2004) [18] note that some candidate features (e.g., "curvature," "intersection") are disputed, and that top-down feature creation complicates the strong nativist reading of FIT.


## Computational & Agent Parallels

### FIT as an Agent Architecture Blueprint

Treisman and Kanwisher (1998) [16] described FIT as a "blueprint for hierarchical information processing" in agents: early layers extract features (like feature maps), and later layers bind them into coherent representations (like focused attention). Multi-modal models that fuse text, images, and tool outputs face the same binding problem that FIT addresses [16].

### Feature Maps and Deep Learning

The hierarchical architecture of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) echoes FIT's feature-map structure: early convolutional layers detect simple features (edges, colors, orientations) with broad receptive fields, while deeper layers combine them into complex object representations [5]. The transformer self-attention mechanism can be seen as a content-addressable binding operation — a "soft" attentional spotlight that combines features across a sequence, which is precisely the operation FIT argued is necessary for coherent perception [4, 5].

### Binding in Multi-Modal AI Systems

Modern multi-modal AI systems face a binding problem: when a vision-language model processes an image and generates text, it must bind visual features to linguistic labels in a coherent way. FIT suggests this binding requires an attentional bottleneck — a claim with implications for architecture design, such as cross-attention layers that explicitly bind visual and linguistic feature maps [16].

### Implications for Agent Monitoring

Change blindness research (Rensink, 2002) — tightly related to FIT — implies that an agent reviewing its own outputs may fail to detect errors if they don't stand out against the overall pattern. Explicit comparison mechanisms (diff-based review) are the computational analog of directed attention to detect changes [4].


## Overlaps & Tensions with Existing Brain Concepts

### Within the Attention Domain

The brain already contains several attention-related pages that intersect with FIT:

- **Attention Networks.md** — FIT's master map and attentional spotlight map onto the dorsal attention network (intraparietal sulcus, frontal eye fields), which implements spatial attention and feature binding. FIT provides the computational *why* for what the dorsal network does.
- **Inattentional-Blindness-Change-Blindness.md** — Change blindness is the failure to detect changes across visual disruptions; it is the natural consequence of FIT's claim that the brain does not maintain a high-resolution snapshot but builds representations on-demand through attentional binding. Without attention directed at the changing location, the change goes unnoticed.
- **Load-Theory-Attention.md** (Lavie) — Load Theory proposes that perceptual load determines whether distractors are processed. This is compatible with FIT: high load consumes binding resources, leaving fewer for distractors. However, Load Theory emphasizes *perceptual capacity* rather than *binding* as the bottleneck, creating a tension about whether the limit is at feature detection or feature integration.
- **Working-Memory-Limits.md** — Object files in FIT are a precursor to working memory representations. The capacity limits of working memory (~4 items) may reflect the number of object files that can be simultaneously maintained through sustained attention.
- **Negative-Priming.md** — Negative priming (slower response to a previously ignored distractor) may reflect the inhibition of feature-map locations that were previously suppressed during binding, linking to FIT's claim that attention selects locations on the master map.
- **Value-Driven-Attentional-Capture.md** — If value signals can bias the master map's activation, this would be a top-down modulation of the attentional spotlight, consistent with Guided Search's claim that goals guide attention.
- **Vigilance-Decrement-Sustained-Attention.md** — Sustained attention maintains the attentional spotlight over time. Vigilance decrement may reflect depletion of the binding resource FIT posits, leading to more illusory conjunctions over time.

### Cross-Domain Tensions

- **Binding Problem in Neuroscience** — FIT's binding problem is the visual instantiation of the broader neural binding problem: how do distributed neural populations produce unified percepts? This connects to debates about consciousness (e.g., Graziano's Attention Schema Theory, which posits that awareness *is* the brain's model of attention itself).
- **Predictive Processing** — In predictive processing frameworks, top-down predictions may serve as the "glue" that binds features, potentially reducing the need for spatial attention as the sole binding mechanism. This is a tension with FIT's strong spatial-attention claim.
- **Global Workspace Theory** — Dehaene & Naccache's Global Workspace model posits that conscious access requires global ignition across a frontoparietal network. FIT's focused attention stage may be the visual-specific implementation of global workspace access for bound object representations.


## Open Questions

1. **Is binding purely spatial?** FIT claims binding is location-based, but object-based attention suggests features can be selected by object membership. Whether spatial attention is necessary for binding or just sufficient remains unresolved [15].

2. **What is the neural code for binding?** Does binding require temporal synchrony (the "binding by synchrony" hypothesis of Singer and Gray), convergence onto conjunctive neurons in the parietal cortex, or spatial attention as FIT claims? Evidence exists for all three mechanisms, and they are not mutually exclusive.

3. **Can there be unconscious binding?** FIT implies that without attention, features remain unbound. But some studies show that features can be implicitly bound without awareness, challenging the strong claim that attention is necessary for all binding.

4. **Is the pre-attentive feature set fixed?** Wolfe & Horowitz (2004) [18] note that some candidate "primitive" features are disputed and that observers can learn to search efficiently for dimensions not in FIT's original set (e.g., line arrangement, intersection). How plastic is the pre-attentive vocabulary?

5. **How does binding scale to natural scenes?** Most FIT experiments use simplified artificial displays. Whether the same binding mechanism operates during natural vision — where scenes contain many objects, occlusions, and clutter — is actively debated.

6. **What is the relation between binding and consciousness?** Treisman (1998) [15] argued that attention binds features into consciously accessible objects. But whether binding without consciousness is possible, and whether consciousness requires binding, are open questions that connect FIT to broader consciousness theories.
