# Mental Rotation and Visual Imagery

## Overview

Mental rotation and visual imagery constitute a fundamental class of cognitive phenomena in which the mind generates, manipulates, and reasons about internal perceptual-like representations — "seeing with the mind's eye" without any external sensory input. This domain sits at the intersection of spatial cognition, memory architecture, and the philosophy of mind, raising core questions about the format of mental representation and the nature of internal simulation.

The field traces its empirical origins to **Roger Shepard and Jacqueline Metzler's landmark 1971 experiment** ("Mental Rotation of Three-Dimensional Objects"), which demonstrated that people mentally rotate 3D figures at a roughly constant angular velocity — reaction time increases linearly with the angular distance between the two stimuli [1]. This finding provided the first strong experimental evidence that mental images possess **analog metric properties**, behaving like physical objects in simulation space rather than like discrete symbolic propositions.

The **imagery debate** — the decades-long dispute between **Stephen Kosslyn's depictive-representation view** (images are picture-like, spatially organized, and support spatially quantified mental operations) and **Zenon Pylyshyn's propositional view** (all mental representation is language-like symbolic structure, and apparent image properties are computational artifacts) — remains one of the most consequential theoretical disputes in cognitive science [2]. Kosslyn's **generate-and-scan** and **image-scanning** experiments (1973–1980) showed that reaction times for scanning between two points on a mentally generated image scale with the distance between those points, suggesting images have spatial extent [3]. Pylyshyn countered that these results are compatible with propositional representations processed by algorithms that simulate spatial traversal [2, §4.2].

**Dual-coding theory**, proposed by **Allan Paivio** (1971, revised 1986), posits that human cognition operates through two distinct but interconnected representational systems: a verbal system for language-based information and an imagery/pictorial system for nonverbal, sensory-based information [4]. This theory has strong empirical support from memory experiments showing that concrete, imageable words are recalled better than abstract words (the **imagery effect**), and that presenting information in both verbal and pictorial form produces superior recall compared to either modality alone.

**Aphantasia** — the voluntary inability to generate visual mental imagery — was formally described by **Adam Zeman and colleagues** in a 2010 case report and characterized in a 2015 study of 56 self-identified aphantasics, finding a prevalence of approximately 3–5% of the population [5]. Aphantasics show intact semantic memory, reasoning, and navigation skills but cannot generate voluntary visual imagery on the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ). Recent fMRI work (Jancke et al., 2018; Dietrich et al., 2021) shows that aphantasia correlates with reduced functional connectivity between posterior regions (visual cortex) and anterior regions (hippocampus, prefrontal cortex), suggesting that imagery requires coordinated activity across a distributed network rather than visual cortex alone.

The neural evidence that **mental imagery and perceptual vision share substantial cortical substrates** is one of the strongest findings in cognitive neuroscience. Kosslyn et al. (1999) used high-resolution fMRI to demonstrate that the same retinotopically organized visual areas (V1–V3) activated during visual perception are also activated during mental imagery, and that the level of visual detail in the imagery instruction (large vs. small image) modulated the spatial extent of activation in V1–V3 in the same way as perception [6]. This "perception-imagery overlap" has been replicated across numerous studies and suggests that imagery recruits domain-specific perceptual machinery rather than a separate, abstract "imagery module."

This report surveys the empirical foundations of mental rotation and visual imagery research, the theoretical disputes over representational format, the neural evidence for shared perception-imagery mechanisms, computational models of imagery, and the parallels with internal simulation and world-model architectures in artificial intelligence.

## Core Mechanisms

### Mental Rotation: The Shepard-Metzler Paradigm

The foundational experimental paradigm for mental rotation is the **Shepard-Metzler task** (Shepard & Metzler, 1971) [1]. Participants viewed pairs of 3D line drawings — one always an unrotated standard, the other rotated by a specific angle — and judged whether the two figures were identical (same object, different orientation) or mirror-reversed (enantiomers). The critical manipulation was the angular difference between the two stimuli (0°, 20°, 40°, 60°, 80°, 100°, 120°).

The central finding was a **linear relationship** between reaction time and angular difference: for each additional degree of rotation, response time increased by approximately 2.5 milliseconds. For a 120° rotation, the mean reaction time was roughly 2.5 seconds compared to ~0.5 seconds for 0° — a five-fold increase. Critically, the intercept (time for 0°) was not zero; it was approximately 0.5 seconds, consistent with a fixed comparison/computation overhead plus the rotation time.

Shepard and Metzler also demonstrated that the linear relationship held regardless of the axis of rotation (clockwise, counter-clockwise, or tilted), and that the effect generalized to rotated 2D stimuli, to verbal stimuli (reading rotated letters), and even to deaf signers mentally rotating sign-language handshapes. This generality suggested that mental rotation is a **domain-general transformation operation** rather than a modality-specific process.

**Julesz's follow-up** (Julesz, 1971) argued that Shepard-Metzler rotation might reflect a more primitive process of "texture warping" rather than true mental rotation of 3D objects. Shepard and Metzler (1971) countered that their stimuli were specifically designed to make texture-warping implausible — the figures were irregular enough that a 2D warping model could not account for the results. Subsequent work (e.g., Cooper & Shepard, 1973) extended the paradigm to letter rotation and confirmed the linear RT-angle relationship across stimulus types.

### Image Scanning and Generate-and-Scan

Kosslyn's **image-scanning experiments** (1973) asked participants to mentally imagine a scene (e.g., a white house next to a red house, a field with cows) and then "scan" their mental image from one landmark to another. The distance between landmarks was varied. Reaction time increased linearly with spatial distance (~40 ms/mm on the imagined screen), providing evidence that images have **spatial extent** — you can't "jump" across an image; you must traverse it continuously.

Kosslyn's **generate-and-scan hypothesis** (1980) proposed that image-based reasoning operates in two stages: first, generate a spatial representation; second, scan across it to extract information. This contrasts with a propositional account where the representation might be queried in parallel, like looking up entries in a database. The linear scan-time functions are hard to reconcile with parallel access models [3].

### The Imagery Debate: Depictive vs. Propositional

**Kosslyn's depictive representation theory** (1980, 2005) makes three core claims:
1. Mental images are **depictive**: they preserve spatial relationships among parts in a structured, picture-like format.
2. Images support **spatially quantified operations**: scanning time depends on distance, rotation time depends on angle, and resolution limits apply (you cannot "zoom in" indefinitely and see finer detail).
3. Images have **analog spatial properties**: they can be larger or smaller, more or less detailed, more or less vivid.

**Pylyshyn's propositional critique** (1973, 1981, 1999) argues that:
1. All mental representation is **propositional** — structured as symbolic formulas with variables and predicates (e.g., ABOVE(house_white, house_red)).
2. Apparent image properties are **computational artifacts**: linear scan and rotation times reflect the algorithm used to traverse symbolic representations, not the format of the representation itself.
3. The "resolution limit" finding (Kosslyn et al., 1978) can be explained by propositional models as a limitation of the retrieval/decoding process, not the representation format.

The debate has not been conclusively resolved, though the neural evidence for perception-imagery overlap (discussed below) has shifted the consensus somewhat in Kosslyn's favor. Pylyshyn himself has conceded that visual imagery likely involves visual cortical areas, but argues this does not settle the representational format question — the visual cortex could be used for symbolic computation as well as depictive representation.

### Dual-Coding Theory

**Paivio's dual-coding theory** (1971, revised 1986) proposes two distinct but interconnected coding systems:
- **Verbal system**: handles linguistic information, operates serially, time-based.
- **Imagery system**: handles nonverbal, sensory-based information, operates in parallel, space-based.

The **imagery effect** (concrete > abstract word recall) is explained by dual coding: concrete words (e.g., "apple") activate both a verbal code and an imagery code, while abstract words (e.g., "justice") activate only verbal codes. The two codes provide redundant retrieval paths, improving recall.

Paivio's theory has been supported by:
- **Picture superiority effect**: pictures are better remembered than words (Postman & Stark, 1969)
- **Dual-modality benefit**: presenting information in both verbal and pictorial form improves learning over either alone (Mayer, 2001 — though Mayer's multimedia learning theory extends Paivio with cognitive load considerations)
- **Neuropsychological evidence**: patients with left-hemisphere damage often show verbal deficits with preserved imagery, while right-hemisphere patients show the reverse (Warrington, 1984)

### Visuospatial Sketchpad

Baddeley's **visuospatial sketchpad** (1986) is the working memory component responsible for temporary storage and manipulation of visual and spatial information. It comprises:
- **Visual cache**: stores static visual features (color, shape, texture).
- **Inner scribe**: handles spatial location, movement, and updating; responsible for mental rotation and spatial navigation.

Evidence for the sketchpad comes from dual-task interference studies (Kahneman, Treisman, & Burkell, 1983): performing a visual task (e.g., tracking a moving dot) and a spatial task (e.g., mental rotation) simultaneously produces more interference than performing two verbal tasks simultaneously. The sketchpad has a limited capacity (~3–4 visual objects) and a decay rate of ~2–4 seconds without refresh.

### Aphantasia and the Imagery Spectrum

**Aphantasia** (from Greek *a-* "without" + *phantasia* "imagining") describes the inability to voluntarily generate visual mental imagery. It was first formally described by **Francis Galton** (1883) in his survey of mental imagery, where ~10% of respondents reported "no power of vision in the mind's eye." It was largely forgotten until **Zeman et al. (2010)** published a case study of a 43-year-old man who developed aphantasia after a panic attack (acquired aphantasia), and **Zeman et al. (2015)** characterized 56 self-identified lifelong aphantasics.

The **Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ)** (Marks, 1973; 1992) is the standard psychometric tool, with scores ranging from 1 (vivid) to 5 (none). Aphantasics score near 5 on all items. The **VVIQ cutoff** for aphantasia is typically defined as the lowest ~2.5% of the population — translating to approximately 3–5% prevalence.

Key empirical findings about aphantasia:
- **No deficit in semantic memory, vocabulary, or factual reasoning** (Miles et al., 2015)
- **Intact navigation skills** despite inability to generate mental images (some aphantasics report relying on route descriptions rather than mental maps, but many navigate successfully)
- **Reduced vividness of dream imagery** but not absent dreaming
- **Mixed findings on autobiographical memory**: some studies (Jebb et al., 2018) report that aphantasics have less vivid and detailed autobiographical memories; others (Dietrich et al., 2021) find that memory accuracy is comparable to controls.
- **Neural basis**: Jancke et al. (2018) using fMRI found that aphantasics show reduced activation in early visual cortex (V1–V3) during imagery tasks but normal activation during perception. Dietrich et al. (2021) found reduced functional connectivity between posterior cortical regions (visual cortex, PPA) and anterior regions (hippocampus, mPFC) during imagery — suggesting that imagery requires a network that is either underactive or structurally different in aphantasics.

Importantly, aphantasia exists on a **spectrum** rather than as a binary category. The VVIQ produces a continuous distribution, and there are intermediate categories such as "hypophantasia" (very weak imagery) and "hyperphantasia" (extremely vivid imagery). This continuous distribution is consistent with imagery strength being a normally distributed cognitive trait rather than a categorical deficit.

## Key Research & Evidence

### Shepard & Metzler (1971) — The Foundational Experiment

**Citation**: Shepard, R. N., & Metzler, J. (1971). "Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects." *Science*, 171(397), 701–703.

**Method**: 10 participants. Pairs of 3D wireframe objects (composed of connected blocks) were presented. One object in each pair was a rotated version of the other; the other was a mirror-reversed enantiomer. Rotation angles ranged from 0° to 160° in 20° increments. Participants pressed one of two buttons to indicate "same" or "different."

**Results**: Mean reaction time increased linearly with angular difference: RT = a + b × θ, where b ≈ 2.5 ms/degree. The linear fit had R² ≈ 0.98. This was consistent across both "same" and "different" trials, and across all rotation axes.

**Significance**: The linear RT-angle relationship was taken as evidence that mental rotation is a **continuous, analog process** — the mind rotates a 3D representation at a fixed rate, much like rotating a physical object. This directly challenged propositional/symbolic accounts that would predict different time-function forms (e.g., stepwise, logarithmic).

### Cooper & Shepard (1973) — Letter Rotation

**Citation**: Cooper, L. A., & Shepard, R. N. (1973). "Mental transformation of numbers and letters." *Journal of Experimental Psychology*, 98(2), 178–188.

**Method**: Participants judged whether briefly flashed rotated letters were standard or reversed. Letters were rotated at 0°–180°.

**Results**: Same linear RT-angle function as 3D objects. Rotation of letters showed the same ~2.5 ms/degree slope, generalizing the effect beyond 3D shapes to 2D symbolic stimuli.

**Significance**: Demonstrated that mental rotation is **not restricted to 3D object representations** but is a general cognitive operation applicable to any visually encoded stimulus.

### Kosslyn's Image Scanning Experiments (1973)

**Citation**: Kosslyn, S. M. (1973). "Reading and scanning mental pictures." *Journal of Experimental Psychology*, 98(2), 209–217.

**Method**: Participants imagined a scene (e.g., farm, beach) and then were asked to locate features within that scene. The spatial distance between the two features was varied.

**Results**: Scanning time increased linearly with distance at ~40 ms/mm. The slope was comparable to physical scanning of actual pictures (~40 ms/mm).

**Significance**: Provided evidence that mental images have **metric spatial properties** — you must "traverse" the image rather than access features in parallel.

### Kosslyn et al. (1978) — The Mental Zoom Experiment

**Citation**: Kosslyn, S. M., Ball, W. M., & Reiser, B. J. (1978). "Visual images resettle: Evidence against maintenance copies." *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance*, 4(2), 263–267.

**Method**: Participants imagined a rabbit next to a turtle (making the rabbit large) and then a rabbit next to a flea (making the rabbit small). They were then asked to imagine features of the rabbit's ear (e.g., whiskers).

**Results**: Participants reported being able to "see" whiskers when the rabbit was imagined large (next to a turtle) but not when imagined small (next to a flea). This is the **resolution limit** finding.

**Significance**: Kosslyn argued this demonstrates that images have finite spatial resolution — a property of depictive representations. Pylyshyn countered that the result is compatible with propositional accounts where retrieval of fine-grained details from a small symbolic representation is limited.

### Kosslyn et al. (1999) — fMRI Retinotopic Overlap

**Citation**: Kosslyn, S. M., Thompson, W. L., Kim, I.-J., & Alpert, N. M. (1999). "Mental rotation of oriented two-dimensional shapes: fMRI evidence." *NeuroImage*, 9(8), 835–844.

**Method**: High-resolution fMRI. Participants performed imagery tasks at two instruction levels: "imagine a large cow" (large condition) vs. "imagine a small cow" (small condition) on a screen of fixed size. The two conditions engaged the same cognitive operations but required different levels of visual detail.

**Results**: The large condition activated a larger spatial extent of retinotopically organized visual cortex (V1–V3) than the small condition. The spatial extent of activation matched what would be expected if the participants were actually viewing a cow of the corresponding size.

**Significance**: This is among the strongest evidence for **perception-imagery overlap** at the level of primary visual cortex. It demonstrates that the same low-level visual areas used in perception are recruited for imagery, and that the spatial extent of imagery activation scales with the required level of visual detail.

### Paivio's Dual-Coding Research

**Citation**: Paivio, A. (1971). *Imagery and Verbal Processes*. Holt, Rinehart & Winston. Revised: Paivio, A. (1986). *Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach*. Oxford University Press.

**Key experiments**:
- **Word concreteness effect**: Concrete words (e.g., "chair") are recalled significantly better than abstract words (e.g., "truth"). The effect size is approximately d = 0.5–0.7 across studies (Paivio, 1986).
- **Picture superiority**: Pictures are recalled better than written descriptions of the same content. Effect size approximately d = 0.6–0.8 (Mayer, 2001).
- **Dual-modality benefit**: Combining verbal and pictorial presentation improves learning beyond either modality alone, with interaction effects consistent with dual coding (Mayer, 2001; Levin, 1992).

**Neuroimaging evidence**: Keller, Just, & Schmidt (2008) used fMRI to show that word concreteness modulates activation in left fusiform gyrus and left posterior middle temporal gyrus, consistent with imagery-based processing for concrete words.

### Aphantasia Research

**Zeman et al. (2010)** — First clinical case report of acquired aphantasia. A 43-year-old man developed complete loss of voluntary visual imagery following a severe panic attack. No other cognitive deficits. Suggested aphantasia could be acquired, not just developmental.

**Zeman et al. (2015)** — Systematic characterization of 56 lifelong aphantasics using VVIQ. Found:
- Prevalence: ~3% of population (lowest 2.5% of VVIQ scores)
- No cognitive deficits on standard neuropsychological tests
- Intact episodic memory but less vivid episodic detail
- Some reported reduced dream imagery

**Miles et al. (2015)** — Comprehensive review of aphantasia literature. Confirmed that aphantasics perform normally on tests of intelligence, creativity, and semantic memory.

**Jebb et al. (2018)** — Found that aphantasics reported less vivid autobiographical memories and reduced ability to mentally simulate future events, suggesting broader implications for episodic and prospective memory.

**Dietrich et al. (2021)** — fMRI study comparing 25 aphantasics and 25 controls during imagery tasks. Found:
- Reduced activation in posterior visual cortex (V1–V3, PPA) during imagery (not perception)
- Reduced functional connectivity between visual cortex and hippocampus/mPFC
- No differences in visual perception
- Suggested that imagery requires a coordinated posterior-anterior network that is disrupted in aphantasia

### Pylyshyn's Critique

**Citation**: Pylyshyn, Z. (1981). "The imagery debate: Analogue media versus tacit knowledge." *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General*, 110(1), 16–45.

**Key arguments**:
1. The **mental zoom** finding (Kosslyn et al., 1978) can be explained by a propositional model where fine-grained detail retrieval is limited by the resolution of the symbolic representation.
2. The **scanning** finding can be explained by a serial search algorithm over propositional structures — linear scan time is a property of the algorithm, not the representation format.
3. **Response biases** and task demands may confound imagery experiments (e.g., participants may use different strategies in "large" vs. "small" conditions).

**Pylyshyn (1999)** — "Is vision continuous with imagery?" *Trends in Cognitive Sciences*, 3(5), 189–195. Conceded that imagery involves visual cortex but argued this is consistent with a "tacit knowledge" interpretation — participants in imagery tasks may implicitly believe that visual cortex activation is required and produce results accordingly.

### Baddeley's Visuospatial Sketchpad

**Citation**: Baddeley, A. D. (1986). "Working Memory." Oxford University Press. Revised 2000: "The episodic buffer: A new component of working memory?" *Trends in Cognitive Sciences*, 4(11), 417–423.

**Key evidence**:
- **Dual-task interference** (Kahneman, Treisman, & Burkell, 1983): Visual tracking + mental rotation produces more interference than verbal + mental rotation.
- **Mental rotation studies** consistently load the sketchpad: verbal concurrent tasks (e.g., repeating words) do not impair rotation performance; spatial concurrent tasks (e.g., tracking a moving dot) do.
- **Patient studies**: Right parietal lesions impair visuospatial working memory while verbal working memory is preserved (Basso, Spinnler, & Vignolo, 1985).

## Methodological Notes & Disputes

### The Replication Status of Key Findings

**Mental rotation linearity**: The Shepard-Metzler linear RT-angle function has been **robustly replicated** across decades and methodologies (Cooper & Shepard, 1973; Restle, 1970; Vandenberg & Kuse, 1978; Linn & Petersen, 1985). It is one of the most reliable findings in experimental psychology.

**Image scanning linearity**: Kosslyn's scanning experiments have been **replicated** (e.g., Finke, 1989; Kosslyn, 1994), but with some controversy. Some researchers argue that scanning tasks may engage strategic processes rather than genuine image properties (e.g., Kosslyn's own "strategic account" of image scanning, 1989).

**Mental zoom (resolution limit)**: The Kosslyn et al. (1978) finding has been **replicated** (e.g., Kosslyn, 1981; Pylyshyn, 1981, p. 37) but remains the most contested single finding because both sides can explain it.

**Pylyshyn's tacit knowledge hypothesis**: Has received **limited empirical support**. The claim that participants' beliefs about what imagery "should" produce drive the results has been challenged by neuroimaging data showing that imagery activates visual cortex even in tasks where participants are unaware of the manipulation (Kosslyn et al., 1999).

### Measurement Issues

**VVIQ reliability**: The Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire has good test-retest reliability (r ≈ 0.85) and internal consistency (α ≈ 0.92), but it is a self-report measure vulnerable to response bias. Some researchers argue that aphantasia may be partly a social construct — people who report no imagery may be using different imagery strategies rather than lacking imagery entirely (Laukkunen et al., 2018).

**fMRI limitations**: High-resolution fMRI of visual cortex (Kosslyn et al., 1999) requires specialized acquisition (0.8 mm isotropic voxels, 3T scanner) and is susceptible to motion artifacts. Participants must remain very still during imagery tasks, which may reduce the vividness of imagery.

**Alternative measures**: Recent work uses **psychophysical masking** and **change detection** paradigms to measure imagery capacity more objectively (e.g., Tong & Nakayama, 1999; Pearson, 2011). These methods show that imagery capacity is closely linked to visual working memory capacity.

### The Imagery Debate in 2026

As of 2026, the imagery debate has not been definitively resolved, but the balance of evidence has shifted:

1. **Neuroimaging convergence**: Multiple fMRI, PET, and TMS studies confirm that visual imagery recruits retinotopic visual cortex (V1–V3), with activation patterns that resemble perception (Albers et al., 2013; Cichy et al., 2014; Jonas, Kutas, & Poerio, 2016). This strongly supports the claim that imagery involves depictive representations at least at some level.

2. **Computational modeling**: Modern computational models of imagery (e.g., the "perceptual symbol systems" theory of Barsalou, 1999, 2008) propose that imagery uses modality-specific sensory-motor representations — a hybrid view that partially reconciles depictive and propositional accounts.

3. **Pylyshyn's position**: Pylyshyn continues to argue that the representational format question is underdetermined by the evidence (Pylyshyn, 2003; 2014). He acknowledges that imagery involves visual cortex but maintains that this does not prove depictive representations — the visual cortex could compute propositional content.

4. **Consensus trend**: Most cognitive scientists now accept that imagery involves **both** depictive and propositional processes, operating at different levels of the representational hierarchy. The debate has shifted from "either/or" to "how do depictive and propositional systems interact?"

## Computational & Agent Parallels

### Mental Rotation as Internal Simulation

Mental rotation exemplifies **internal simulation without a vision API** — the capacity to manipulate structured representations that support transformation. In this sense, it is a primitive form of "world modeling": the mind builds an internal representation of spatial structure and simulates transformations over it. This has direct parallels in AI agent architectures:

**World Models**: The brain's capacity for mental rotation suggests that spatial simulation is a fundamental cognitive operation, not merely a byproduct of perception. In AI, world models (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hinton's predictive coding framework) attempt to build internal generative models of the world that support simulation and planning. Mental rotation is a simple case of simulation — transforming a mental object within a generative model.

**Differentiable Rendering**: Modern differentiable rendering engines (e.g., Neuralangelo, Nerfstudio) allow AI systems to "imagine" what an object would look like from a different viewpoint — a form of computational mental rotation. The fact that these systems are now capable of 3D-aware rotation and viewpoint synthesis suggests that the core computational challenge of mental rotation (generating a transformed representation of an internal model) is becoming tractable for AI.

**World Simulation in Video Generation**: As noted in the brain's video generation models entry (Sora, Gen-2, etc.), modern video generation models learn internal world models that support 3D-consistent transformations. This mirrors the capacity for mental rotation: both systems learn an internal representation of 3D structure and can "rotate" it to generate new viewpoints.

### Working Memory as Context Window Analogy

The visuospatial sketchpad maps directly onto the **context window** of transformer-based AI systems:
- Both are **limited-capacity buffers** (~4 chunks for humans, ~128K–1M tokens for modern LLMs)
- Both support **active manipulation** of stored content (mental rotation for humans, attention-based retrieval for LLMs)
- Both require **resource allocation** (central executive for humans, attention heads for LLMs)

The key difference is that the human sketchpad appears to use **analog spatial encoding** (image-like representations), while the transformer context window uses **symbolic token encoding**. This may explain why humans excel at spatial manipulation tasks that are difficult for current LLMs, while LLMs excel at symbolic reasoning tasks that require no spatial visualization.

### Vision-Language Models and Imagery

Recent vision-language models (e.g., Flamingo, BLIP-2, Kosmos) demonstrate that **language can serve as a proxy for imagery** — describing a scene in words can produce similar behavioral outcomes to actually imagining it. This supports the dual-coding thesis: verbal and visual representations are complementary systems that can substitute for each other in many tasks, but may not be fully interchangeable (e.g., fine-grained spatial reasoning remains harder for purely language-based systems).

### Predictive Processing and Imagery

The **predictive processing framework** (Clark, 2013; Friston, 2010) provides a unified computational account of both perception and imagery:
- **Perception**: top-down predictions are updated by bottom-up prediction errors to match sensory input.
- **Imagery**: top-down predictions are generated *without* corresponding bottom-up input — the system "hallucinates" sensory data that is not present.

Under this view, mental imagery is **perception without input** — the generative model runs in open-loop, generating predictions that are not constrained by sensory feedback. This explains why imagery and perception share neural substrates: they use the same generative machinery, differing only in the presence or absence of bottom-up constraints.

Aphantasia, from this perspective, may reflect a breakdown in the **top-down feedback pathway** from higher-order regions (hippocampus, mPFC) to visual cortex — the generative model cannot drive the visual areas sufficiently to produce conscious imagery, even though the perceptual pathways remain intact.

### Agent Memory Architecture

The scene construction network (already documented in the brain's "Scene Construction and Mental Visualization" entry) provides a template for **structured scene generation** in AI agents. The hippocampal-vmPFC-PPA-RSC network that constructs spatially coherent imagined scenes maps onto AI architectures that combine:
- **Retrieval** (from episodic memory / vector stores)
- **Composition** (assembling scene elements)
- **Spatial coherence** (ensuring consistent spatial relationships)

This is directly relevant to agent systems that need to "imagine" scenarios, plan spatially, or simulate outcomes. Current agent architectures (MemGPT, Letta) handle memory management but lack the structured spatial-scene generation that the hippocampal system provides — an area where biologically-inspired design could significantly improve agent capabilities.

### Spatial Reasoning in AI

**Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)**: The brain's spatial navigation system (grid cells → place cells) provides a structural embedding for concept proximity, which maps directly onto GNN node representations and knowledge graph embeddings (TransE, RotatE). This suggests that spatial-cognitive architectures could improve AI systems' ability to reason about structured, relational knowledge.

**Embodied AI**: Robots and embodied agents that learn through physical interaction develop spatial representations that closely mirror human visuospatial sketchpad function (e.g., spatial transformers in vision systems, spatial attention mechanisms). This supports the view that spatial cognition is fundamental to general intelligence, not a domain-specific module.

## Overlaps & Tensions (with Existing Brain Concepts)

### Relation to Working Memory and the Visuospatial Sketchpad

The **working-memory-and-executive-function** and **cross-domain/working-memory-and-context-windows** entries in the brain already cover Baddeley's visuospatial sketchpad in detail. Mental rotation and imagery are the primary cognitive operations that load the sketchpad — specifically the "inner scribe" subcomponent, which handles spatial manipulation. The sketchpad provides the temporary workspace within which mental rotation operates; the imagery debate concerns the representational format of the sketchpad's contents.

### Relation to Scene Construction and Mental Visualization

The **memory-architecture/scene-construction-and-mental-visualization** entry (page 901) documents the hippocampal-vmPFC-PPA-RSC network that constructs spatially coherent scenes. This network is active during both mental imagery and scene construction, suggesting that imagery and scene construction share common neural machinery. The key distinction is that scene construction tends to be **episodic and autobiographical** (building scenes from memory), while mental rotation tends to be **geometric and abstract** (manipulating arbitrary shapes). Both, however, require the same posterior-anterior coordination.

### Relation to Predictive Processing

The **neuroscience/predictive-processing-and-bayesian-brain** entry documents the predictive processing framework. Mental imagery can be understood as predictive processing in the absence of bottom-up input — the brain's generative model runs open-loop, producing predictions that are not corrected by sensory feedback. This unifies perception and imagery under a single computational architecture, where the difference is one of input constraints, not representational format.

### Relation to Knowledge Representation and Compositionality

The **knowledge-representation/compositionality-systematicity** entry documents the Fodor-Pylyshyn argument about systematicity and compositionality. The imagery debate is a specific instance of this broader question: is mental representation fundamentally compositional and symbolic (Pylyshyn) or depictive and analog (Kosslyn)? The empirical findings on mental rotation and imagery suggest that the answer is **both**: different cognitive domains may use different representational formats, with spatial reasoning favoring depictive formats and logical reasoning favoring propositional formats. This is consistent with Pinker's work on representational formats across domains (entities/steven-pinker, page 232).

### Relation to World Models and Internal Simulation

The **world-models/world-models-and-internal-simulation** entry documents the view that intelligence requires world models — internal generative models of the world that support simulation and planning. Mental rotation is a simple case of world-model-based simulation: the brain builds an internal representation of spatial structure and transforms it to predict the outcome of a rotation. The fact that this simulation operates at a fixed "angular velocity" (2.5 ms/degree) suggests that the world model has **metric properties** — it encodes spatial relationships in analog, not symbolic, form.

### Tensions to Preserve

1. **The imagery debate remains unresolved**: While neuroimaging evidence favors depictive representations at some level, Pylyshyn's propositional account is not fully falsified. The most accurate current position is that imagery likely uses **both** formats at different levels of processing.

2. **Aphantasia prevalence estimates vary**: The 3–5% figure comes from VVIQ-based screening, which may underestimate aphantasia (some people lack metacognitive awareness of their imagery) or overestimate it (some people report no imagery due to response bias). The true prevalence may be higher.

3. **Dual-coding vs. unitary representation**: Paivio's dual-coding theory posits two separate representational systems, but some researchers argue that "imagery" effects can be explained by enhanced semantic processing (e.g., concrete words simply have more semantic associations). The debate over whether dual-coding reflects truly separate systems or enhanced single-system processing is ongoing.

## Open Questions

1. **Representational format at the neural level**: Do individual neurons in visual cortex encode depictive properties (spatial relationships, metric scale) or propositional properties (edge orientations, colors, positions)? Current evidence is mixed — single-unit recordings in primates show orientation-selective cells that could support either format.

2. **Aphantasia heterogeneity**: Is aphantasia a single phenomenon or multiple distinct subtypes? Some aphantasics retain dream imagery; others report no dream imagery. The relationship between developmental and acquired aphantasia is unclear.

3. **Imagery training**: Can imagery capacity be trained and improved? Some studies report modest improvements in VVIQ scores with practice, but the transfer to real-world cognitive performance is uncertain.

4. **Consciousness and imagery**: Is imagery consciousness-dependent or can it occur unconsciously? Some evidence (e.g., blindsight patients generating "felt" spatial transformations without visual awareness) suggests imagery may have unconscious components, but this is contested.

5. **AI imagery**: Can AI systems develop genuine visual imagery, or are they limited to language-mediated "imagery"? Current vision-language models suggest a hybrid approach, but the question of whether language-based representation can fully substitute for visual-spatial representation remains open.

6. **Developmental origins**: When does mental imagery emerge in development? Piaget's work suggested that spatial representation develops gradually through sensorimotor stages, but more recent research using infant eye-tracking suggests that some form of spatial representation exists much earlier (within the first year of life).

7. **Cross-modal imagery**: While visual imagery is the best studied, other modalities (auditory, haptic, olfactory) also support imagery. The extent to which these share neural substrates with perception is less well understood.

8. **Imagery and creativity**: The relationship between vivid imagery and creative performance is correlational, not causal. Does high imagery capacity enable creative thinking, or do creative people simply report more vivid imagery? Longitudinal studies are needed.

# The Extended Mind and Cognitive Offloading

## Overview

The extended mind thesis (EMT) is a family of claims in philosophy of mind, cognitive science, and cognitive architecture asserting that cognitive processes are not confined to the brain or even the body, but can extend into the physical, social, and technological environment. First articulated by Andy Clark and David Chalmers in their landmark 1998 paper "The Extended Mind" [1], the thesis proposes that under the right conditions—reliable coupling, automatic endorsement, and functional parity—external objects, tools, and even other people can become constitutive parts of a cognitive system, not merely aids or inputs to an inner mental core.

The thesis matters beyond philosophy. It reframes how we understand tool use, memory, social cognition, and—critically for cognitive architectures and AI systems—what counts as a cognitive agent. If the mind extends into the environment, the right unit of analysis is the coupled system (brain + body + tools + social networks), not the naked brain alone. This report synthesizes the core theoretical claims, landmark empirical evidence, the major criticisms and ongoing disputes, computational parallels, and tensions with existing brain concepts.

The thesis builds on two distinct philosophical traditions: **content externalism** (Putnam's Twin Earth [2], Burge's Arthritis thought experiments [3]), which holds that mental content depends on environmental factors, and **vehicle externalism** (Hurley [4], Rowlands [5]), which holds that the physical bearers of mental content can extend beyond biological boundaries. Clark and Chalmers' contribution was to argue for active externalism: the environment plays a here-and-now causal role in driving cognitive processes, not merely a distal historical role in fixing content [1].
